summary: Specifies the format of ARPA Internet text messages, such as headers and addressing. It revises RFC 733 and removes features that did not gain acceptance. Replaced by RFC 2822.

plainLanguage.summary: The layout of an email: who it is from, who it is to, a subject, then the message. This is the standard form for that layout.

questions: what does an email header look like
subtitle: The 1982 standard for what an email message looks like: header fields, a blank line, then the body.

tldr.problem: Networked mail programs on the ARPA Internet needed one agreed layout for the text of a message, so that messages from different hosts could be read and routed the same way.
tldr.mechanism: A message is a set of header fields (a name, a colon and a value, one logical line each), then a blank line, then the body. The RFC defines the syntax of the fields, dates and addresses in an augmented BNF.
tldr.outcome: RFC 822 is an Internet Standard that revises RFC 733, but it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2822, which is where the format is defined today.

today: RFC 822 is an Internet Standard, but it has been obsoleted by RFC 2822 and updated by RFC 1123, RFC 1138, RFC 1148, RFC 1327 and RFC 2156. Read the replacement for the current message format.

sections.title: Scope and the Memo Framework
sections.content:
RFC 822 specifies a syntax for text messages sent among computer users within the framework of electronic mail. It supersedes RFC 733, dropping features that failed to gain acceptance, adding a different addressing scheme for inter-network mail and introducing the idea of re-transmission.

The RFC views a message as an envelope plus contents. It covers only the contents. It is also a definition of what is passed between hosts: it does not dictate the formats a site uses internally or how user interface programs behave.

The design is a general memo framework. A rigidly formatted header section comes first, followed by a main part whose format this document does not specify. Header syntax is kept separate from the syntax of individual fields, so a simple parser can find the fields without understanding each one.
sections.plainLanguage: This standard only describes the letter, not the envelope or the post office. It says what the letter must look like when it travels from one computer to another.

sections.title: Fields, Folding and Lexical Tokens
sections.content:
A message consists of header fields and, optionally, a body. The body is a sequence of lines of ASCII characters, separated from the headers by a null line, which is a line with nothing before the CRLF. Each field is a field-name, a colon and a field-body.

Long fields may be folded onto several lines. Wherever linear white space is allowed, a CRLF immediately followed by at least one space or tab may be inserted. Unfolding treats that CRLF plus white space as the white space alone. Lines longer than 65 or 72 characters are commonly considered long, though the standard does not impose a limit.

Fields such as Subject and Comments are plain text. Fields holding dates and addresses are structured. Their bodies are split into atoms, quoted strings, domain-literals, comments and special characters. Comments in parentheses may nest and are ignored by the formal semantics. A backslash quotes a character, but only inside quoted strings, domain-literals and comments, so Full\ Name@Domain is not legal and must be written "Full Name"@Domain.

Field names and most other alphabetic strings are case-insensitive, so From, FROM and FroM are the same field. The local part of an address is case-preserved, with the exception of Postmaster.
sections.plainLanguage: If a line in the form is too long, you can carry on writing on the next line as long as you start it with a space. The computer glues the pieces back together.

sections.title: The Header Fields
sections.content:
Headers are not required to occur in any particular order, except that the body must come after them. The RFC recommends sending them in the order Return-Path, Received, Date, From, Subject, Sender, To, cc and so on. Every message needs a date, an originator and at least one destination field.

  • Trace: Return-Path is added by the final transport system. Each relaying service adds a Received field, which can name the sending host (from), the receiving host (by), the protocol used (with) and the time of receipt.
  • Originator: From is the person who wished the message sent. Sender is the agent that actually sent it and MUST be present when it differs from From. Reply-To says where replies should go.
  • Receivers: To (primary), cc (secondary) and bcc (blind copies, not shown to the other recipients).
  • Reference and other: Message-ID, In-Reply-To, References, Keywords, Subject, Comments and Encrypted.

A field name starting with Resent- has the same meaning as the unprefixed field but marks information added by someone who forwarded the message. Dates look like 20 Jun 82 followed by a time and a zone, such as UT, GMT, EST or an offset in the form of a sign and four digits.

Extension fields defined by later documents will never begin with X-, which leaves that prefix free for user-defined fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has boxes for From, To, Date and Subject. If you pass the letter on to a friend, you add a new set of boxes marked Resent so everyone can see who forwarded it.

sections.title: Addresses and Domains
sections.content:
An address is either a single mailbox or a named group of mailboxes. The common form of a mailbox is local-part@domain, optionally preceded by a human-readable name, as in phrase <addr-spec>. The local part is uninterpreted by everything except the final host. A domain is a series of sub-domains separated by periods, with the top-level domain at the right.

The domain model is a logical hierarchy, tied to name registration rather than to the path a message takes. Within the sender's own sub-domain an address may be abbreviated by leaving off the shared right-hand part, but once a message crosses a domain boundary all addresses must be fully specified.

The RFC also defines a few special forms. A domain-literal such as [10.0.3.19] names a host by its Internet address, and its use is strongly discouraged. A route inside angle brackets provides explicit source routing, which is also discouraged. A group has the form name:mailbox, mailbox; and groups may not be nested.

Finally, the local part Postmaster is reserved: Postmaster@domain is required to be valid at each site, and mail sent to it is routed to a person responsible for the site's mail system, in any mixture of case.
sections.plainLanguage: An email address is like a street address read backwards: the person's name, then an at sign, then the town and country. Every town must have a postmaster, a person you can write to when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 733
sections.content:
Appendix C lists how this standard differs from RFC 733. The main changes are:

  • The Return-path and Received trace fields and the Resent- prefix were added.
  • The Encrypted field was added, along with the rule that extension fields never begin with X-.
  • The period and square brackets became special characters, and domain-literals were introduced.
  • Addressing is now absolute and global, with one at-sign. The string at no longer works as an address delimiter, and the route construct separates path from address.
  • Group lists must have a name and may not be nested, and the date and time zone rules were simplified.

The Postmaster local part was also reserved, so that users are guaranteed at least one valid address at a site.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the rulebook. It threw out the rules nobody followed and added a few new ones, like keeping a trail of who handled the letter.
